#8692. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time.  Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the…

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it)

This line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

One important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Currently “High” and We Want Them Lower

Ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive)

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, new EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About

The funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more quickly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

And “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

JoeO, I don’t think you’re wrong. Perhaps I’m missing something, but every wage/salary stat MMM cites is nominal. To your point, nominal wages do not accurately reflect actual purchasing power. To do that you need to look at real wages.

An AI overview: Real wages are wages that have been adjusted for inflation, while wages are unadjusted. Real wages are a measure of how much a worker can buy with their wages, and are an important indicator of living standards and worker productivity

MMM wrote “wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%”. During 2019 & 2020 inflation was abnormally low 2.3% and 1.4%. Adding these years to the range scews the average. Additionally, no one was expressing concern over the price of goods at that time.

For 2021-2023 inflation was 7%,6.5% and 3.4%. This is when people began voicing concern over prices for obviously valid reasons. So 2021 presents a better starting point. From the BLS data I’ve seen, since 2021 CPI is +20.6%, wages are +19.2% and real wages are -1.1%. Correct me if I’m wrong, but that seems to indicate that purchasing power for the average American has in fact decreased and they are in fact not better off thatn they were four years ago.

Agreed! I think this is the biggest economic myth that needs to be addressed. Autarky is the end goal of all these tariffs, and it has negative economic consequences that seem to be missing from what the politicans say. Without the ability to trade, countries lose the benefits of specialization and comparative advantage. This leads to higher prices for in country consumers and a lack of diversity in available goods. Autarky stifles innovation and technological progress by isolating a country from global competition and advancements. An autarkic system is also more vulnerable to domestic economic shocks, such as natural disasters or supply disruptions, because it cannot rely on imports to balance shortfalls. Autarky reduces a country’s economic growth potential by cutting off access to international markets, foreign investment, and trade-driven employment opportunities. Finally, it risks diplomatic isolation, as trade restrictions often result in retaliatory measures from other nations, further limiting a country’s global economic and political influence. While autarky may appeal in terms of self-reliance, the downsides—higher costs, reduced growth, and vulnerability—make it unsustainable in the modern country.

1. “Government deficits don’t necessarily cause inflation. They are funded by the sale of T-bills and bonds.”

Yes, but if demand for those bonds is weak, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort, printing money to purchase them, which can lead to inflation.

2. “Even an expanding money supply does not dictate the inflation rate. As we saw last year, we can have inflation even when the money supply shrinks, and this year we have much lower inflation even with a growing money supply.”

Yes, but inflation often lags behind changes in the money supply—it can take time for new money to fully circulate and impact prices.

3. “Moderate inflation is NOT bad and does not destroy purchasing power (unless you keep your wealth all in cash).”

Inflation does destroy purchasing power. Investing in assets that grow faster than inflation, like stocks or real estate, can keep you ahead of it. They don’t avoid inflation, they just try to beat it.

Mr. Money Mustache October 30, 2024, 7:23 pm

I think hybrids were great as a transition technology, because they helped our gas cars become more efficient back when batteries were too expensive to make an affordable all-electric car.

For example, in 2013, electric car battery packs cost about $780 per kWh to build, meaning my Tesla Model Y’s 80 kWh pack alone would have cost $62,000!

Today (2024 as I write this) that battery pack number is about $100, so my battery is only $8k of the car’s price. And since an electric car no longer needs an engine, transmission, exhaust system or all the other junk that comes with combustion, we now see electric cars have become LESS expensive than gas cars of equivalent quality/performance (the model Y is in the low $40s brand new, and under $30k used)

With the combination of easy+cheap home charging plus a bunch of nationwide fast charging networks (Tesla’s is still the best by far), there is no reason to have to settle for a hybrid – unless you’re shopping in the cheaper end of the used market. An under $10k used Prius with low miles is still a great frugal car if you can find one!

Avoid Nissan Leafs since their charging standard is no longer used and their batteries are air cooled, leading to far more degradation than other EVs that have active cooling. If you’re looking at Chevy Bolt’s make sure the battery modules were repaired per the recall. One of the best things about them is that your house is your “fuel” station. If you don’t have at home charging available it can be more of a challenge (unless your work has chargers).

Our 2014 Leaf that we bought used for a song in 2019 is still doing exactly what we need it to do – around town car, usually under 10 miles per day (eBike would be even more economical, but I kinda like my climate control here in the very hot, very humid southeast). If you’re needing to do a lot of long-distance driving, then yeah – Leaf’s, particularly older ones aren’t a great choice.

Agreed on at-home charging still the best way – public charging is expanding, but paid public charging is often as expensive as gasoline.

https://www.autotempest.com/ aggregates a bunch of different used car sales websites & has filters to make searching really easy.

Suddenly the recovered economy from the pandemic increased demand, and supply was still low, so fuel prices skyrocketed. Instead of keeping production up, for fear of losing money, or quickly ramping production back up, petroleum producers deliberately dragged their feet in ramping production back up to artificially lower supply to increase prices and make record profits. This is somewhat similar to the DeBeers diamond corporation hoarding diamonds to artificially reduce supply to increase prices and thus profits. The end result is higher prices of everything, since everything is shipped via trucks that use too much fuel. I long for the day when our entire economy doesn’t depend upon a global oil market, when electric tractor trailers deliver goods using electricity generated by solar panels and windmills, but we aren’t there yet unfortunately. I personally work from home as a software engineer, and from the teachings of this blog deliberately live within bicycle distance of the grocery store, so I have minimal fuel costs, however I still feel the effects of fuel costs at the grocery store, from my home builder, other contractors (which is why I try to DIY everything), etc. Car prices went up from chip shortages after covid, like way up. Housing prices when up after covid because people like myself no longer had to live near our high paying jobs and could work remotely from a lower cost of living area, so people suddenly increased demand in the suburban/exurban/semi-rural areas. Business works the way it works. Capitalism works the way it works. No business will deliberately lose money to please its customers, and displease it’s shareholders. To those who think I am a hypocrite, I cite the old saying “if ya can’t beat em, join em” and by them I mean the capitalists.

Great article. This is a misconception I notice all the time, and it’s good to see more high-profile debunkings.

It’s true that politicians can steer the long-term direction of the economy – either with bad policies like immigration restrictions, NIMBY laws and trade wars, or good policies like fixing infrastructure, incentivizing renewable energy and making healthcare affordable.

But far too many people think that the president has a magic wand to control inflation or gas prices. When their lives are going well, they give the party in power too much of the credit, and when their lives are going badly, they give the party in power too much of the blame.

The unfortunate thing about democracy is that most people who study the issues and think carefully have already decided who they’re going to vote for. For politicians to win elections, they have to get the increasingly tiny slice of swing voters – who, by definition, tend to be the people who don’t pay attention to politics or know very much about policy. Thus, those politicians have to pander to swing voters with ideas that don’t make sense but sound good to the uninformed. If us Mustachians were in charge, things would be different.

I’m a city dweller with a desk job, so take this analysis for what its worth. Also, a farm or ranch is a business, so a approaching it from a personal finance perspective may not be the right way to look at it.

From what I understand most small farms and ranches in the US aren’t profitable. Based on my parents’ neighbors and many of the sources I’ve read, I think this is because farming and ranching is often a cultural identity and a lifestyle choice, and these properties aren’t being run as an efficient business. They’re hobby farms run by rich dentists, or their owners identify as “cattle ranchers” whether or not the market supports that identity and without a diversified, efficient business plan to maximize the profitability of the entire enterprise.

Here are some Mustachian principles I think apply to farms, ranches, and people who live in rural areas.

Trade the pickup truck for a smaller, less expensive, and preferably used vehicle that does the job better and drive it as little as possible. For everything else, buy a bike or small (used) sedan. There are shades of rural, but a lot of transportation needs can still be met by bike or electric bike. I rode my ebike about 40 miles yesterday to run errands in the city. I grew up in the sticks, and I’d have had a lot more freedom if I’d had an ebike. An electric cargo bike may able to be substituted for a four-wheeler or pickup truck for a lot of on farm transportation. The bike I have can basically carry the weight of two people. If you’re moving a dozen 40lb bags of feed around, that’s a max of four trips by electric cargo bike. Bikes are low, so loading one is faster and easier than throwing bags up into a pickup truck bed.

When it comes to farm equipment and purchases of all kinds, ask if you really need the equipment or if its just a status symbol. Can the job be done with muscle power. If you need the equipment, can you buy it used or substitute a less flashy alternative. Financing for farm equipment is similar to financing for a new car. Probably a money hole.

Every single farm input needs scrutiny and optimization. Fertilizer that washes into the river is money going down the sewer. This includes water, fertilizer, pesticides, etc. Spraying money at the problem isn’t solving it.

Cut your Cash-Leaking Umbilical Cord. If you moved to the country to enjoy the country, why do you need 500 channels of entertainment?

Focus on your Circle of Control, not your Circle of Interest. You can’t change the global cattle market, but you can decide whether to add sheep and goats, get paid by a land conservancy, host duck hunters, market your beef to yuppies at farmers markets, or do any number of other things to increase the profitability of your property.

Reduce grocery trips and expenses by growing your own food and trading with neighbors. Put in some fruit trees and a kitchen garden. Raise some chickens. Trade for milk. This should be one of the big advantages of living in the countryside in farm country.

That’s just a quick look, but I think a lot of the Mustachian principles apply in rural areas too.

How we feel about AI risk is instructive of where investors often go wrong when dealing with risk. We deal with risk in a very human fashion. We learn from emotive experiences and focus on what is happening right in front of our eyes. We judge risks based on how they make us feel.

Most wealthy retirees either overconfidently blow through their assets (rare) or cautiously refuse to touch the principal (typical). You may have spent years planning to retire at a specific age, only to discover that the timing is not entirely yours to control. The job you assumed would carry you to your planned retirement date may no longer be there, and the financial plan built around that timeline may need to change with it. That is why retirement planning should not depend too heavily on a single age, a specific account balance, or a rigid view of the future.

For couples with a big age gap, the number of moving parts multiplies. Financial planners characterize the process as essentially having to knit together two different retirement trajectories and make it work for one family.

Sometimes we go completely down the personal finance rabbit hole. We use frugality as a weapon. We track every single cent we spend. We obsess over our investments, constantly maximizing the tax code, and agonizing over the minor differences between traditional and Roth accounts. We become so hyper-focused on the efficiency of our financial machine that we forget why we built it in the first place.

The tax benefits of a Health Savings Account (HSA) effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary. That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account in an effort to maximize the tax benefits.

#8685. Debt And Physician Finances

Have you ever had a termite infestation? You likely didn’t realize you did until it was too late. For months or sometimes years, you go about your life without the faintest idea that something is afoot, because after all, the house looks just fine from the driveway.

By the time you notice that sagging floorboards, the structure is already compromised.

Debt is that termite infestation. You don’t realize the damage it’s doing until it’s too late. It gnaws through your income, unnoticed, until the day a job change, a market downturn or an unplanned expense reveals just how rickety the foundation has become.

More than a third of Americans earning $200,000 or more say they’re living paycheck to paycheck. Nearly a third of six-figure earners describe themselves as financially stretched, struggling, or drowning.

Physicians are not exempt from this. A high income means nothing on its own. It can open up opportunities, yes but those options feel out of reach when debt takes away the majority of your paycheck.

Student loans and a primary mortgage are fixtures of adulthood. If you’re a physician and have never had to carry these, you’re extremely lucky. Or you know something I don’t— in which case, please share your secret with the rest of us.

The median education debt for the class of 2025 was $215,000— not including undergraduate loans. Many physicians carry this into their 40s and 50s.

Nobody becomes a doctor debt-free unless family money covers the tab. In return you get to enjoy a career in medicine earning good money with plenty of lucrative options for supplementing that income.

The mortgage on a primary residence is an equally unavoidable aspect of adult finances. In return you get a place to call home and an asset that (usually) appreciates. Mortgage is debt, yes, but paying it down builds equity that would otherwise go to someone else in the form of rent.

This type of debt cannot be categorized as termites. This is the foundation you build on top of and most physicians manage it fine once attending income kicks in. There are also ways to significantly ease the burden on this type of debt.

Credit card balances, car payments beyond what a reliable car would cost, a second home bought at the top of a market, an extravagant vacation you didn’t save for but financed instead— I could go on. These are all examples of bad debt. Not because they aren’t “profitable” but also because the ROI they provide is short-lived.

Having a lake house feels great but not if you have to put up with a toxic workplace in order to pay it off. Jetting off to Switzerland feels like freedom but not if you have to skimp on your 401(k) contributions for the following years in order to pay it off.

In the second quarter of 2026, the average APR on credit card accounts that carry a balance was 22.15%, up from 21.52% in Q1. Total U.S. credit card debt reached $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, closing in on the all-time high of $1.28 trillion set at the end of 2025. Roughly 60% of cardholders carry a balance month to month rather than paying in full.

A $15,000 balance at 22% APR costs over $3,300 a year in interest alone, money that produces nothing, builds nothing and simply vanishes. Extended across a decade of minimum payments, the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase several times over.

A 43-year-old high-earner drowning in debt posted his story on Reddit. Let’s call him Bill.

“On the outside, I probably look like a success. On the inside, I feel like I’m slowly breaking — just getting through one day at a time,” he wrote.

Him and his spouse carry close to $1 million in combined loans. Both work high-paying jobs. On paper, they look fine. In practice, their special-needs son’s therapy costs $3,000 a month. Before his diagnosis, that $3000 was the extra income they had planned to put towards paying down debt. These are the kind of curveballs life can throw at you. Out of nowhere, unannounced— thwack.

Bill tried his hand at several side businesses which failed and added more debt on top. He describes feeling trapped in a career he doesn’t enjoy with no visible exit.

Close to $1 million is debt may sound insane but in New York, D.C. or California, that number is an easy target. HCOL is no joke and Bill’s situation isn’t unique. Debt can be enticing even to the best of us.

Bill’s failure stems from the fact that he had thought nothing would ever go wrong and he would be able to pay off

the debt from the extra income. It was that years of “should be fine” income had never been forced into a written plan, so a single disruption ate the entire buffer.

That’s the sinkhole version of debt. It doesn’t look like reckless spending from the outside. It looks like a normal life that happens to be standing on ground with nothing underneath it.

Also read: Is Driving a Honda Smarter Than Flexing a Ferrari?

We love compound interest but not when it’s on the other side. Compound interest grows our savings the same way it grows balances— with indifferent efficiency.

Every month a balance carries over at 20%+ APR, that growth compounds against the borrower. Over 20 years, that comes out to 52.83x of the original number which could easily mean the difference between a paid-off house and a large credit card bill that never seems to shrink.

Every debt payment carries two costs. The first is obvious: the dollars leaving the account each month. The second almost never gets counted, because it never shows up anywhere: opportunity cost.

The cost of what you give up when your dollars go towards debt when they could’ve gone towards something profitable.

Consider a physician making aggressive payments on $215,000 in student loans during the first years as an attending.

Once the balance hits zero, that monthly cash flow can now go towards investment instead of paying a loan servicer. It can now be invested in index funds, a retirement account or a rental property that produces income instead of consuming it.

Also read: Building Wealth: Lessons In Sustainable Investment for Physicians

That’s what makes debt a double hit. Stretched across a 30-year investing timeline, missed growth frequently outweighs the interest itself, sometimes by a wide margin.

That’s why many advisors suggest building a straightforward financial foundation before reaching for anything advanced. Boring, broadly diversified investing beats clever debt-servicing strategies almost every time because it lets compounding start earlier instead of later.

The next time you sit down to fine-time your financial plan, consider the following:

Learn more: Is Diversification Finally Working Again?

After a decade of deferred spending, attending income brings much-need relief. But with it, comes the temptation to catch up all at once.

Those one-third of six-figure households that feel “stretched, struggling, or drowning” I mentioned earlier?

Their biggest downfall is precisely the fact that every income jump they are blessed with gets absorbed by a bigger house, a nicer car and a few thousand extra dollars a year in subscriptions and shopping. The brokerage accounts become the stepchildren that never get any love or attention.

Don’t be the evil stepmother. Do this instead:

Everyone takes stress as a given. As children we’re conditioned to worry about our homework and grades, as we grow older, we worry about fitting in, dating and winning the rat race.

The joys of parenthood are symbiotic with the worries of how to raise and protect our children in a world like ours. Being alive is, in essence, being stressed.

Debt adds in another layer of stress to all of that. But this is one we usually push away to the back of our minds so much so that it stops registering as stress at all.

Anyone carrying a meaningful balance knows what I’m talking about. Unexpected car repairs make us flinch. Due dates feel heavy but they arrive and we pay; then do it again the following month. Progress feels theoretical.

A systematic review of 39 U.S. studies found that debt is consistently linked to higher rates of stress and even suicide. The authors pointed to financial strain and the pressure of collection as the major drivers. Some debt, such as a mortgage, was labeled as “secure” which proves the point that not all debt is bad.

Another study reports that over-indebted consumers have lower life satisfaction and poorer health due to a diminished sense of control.

Eventually the discomfort becomes the baseline, and that’s when people take on more debt, because an actual plan to eliminate it no longer feels realistic.

Financing makes this worse by design. Nearly every major purchase now arrives with a monthly payment option built in, because a payment feels smaller than a price tag even when the total cost is higher.

47% of Buy Now, Pay Later users have been late on at least one loan in the past year. That percentage had been rising steadily, as it was 41% in 2025 and just 34% in 2024.

More alarmingly, 54% of consumers say that they wouldn’t be able to make ends meet without these loans. 29% say they use them to pay for groceries.

Financial well-being research consistently finds that experiences with debt and credit correlate directly with how secure people feel about their finances, independent of income.

So the relief once you’re on the other side? It’s exhilarating.

A Gallup study found that among recent graduates, only 25% of those with more than $50,000 in debt were thriving financially compared to 40% of debt-free grads.

Physicians who’ve finished paying off credit cards or student loans, especially after years of aggressive payments alongside PSLF, will know what I’m talking about. The financial change is expected but the psychological weight lifting is what often catches you off guard.

If you want to experience that relief sooner rather than later, stick to aggressive repayment and steer clear of financing anything marketed by its monthly payment instead of its total cost.

Debt is sneaky like that. It can make you feel like you’re living your best life, doing better than ever— doing better than those around you. It’s a costly little dog and pony show.

Home equity products are the easiest way to explain this. A physician spends years building equity in a primary residence, then starts seeing offers to unlock that equity through a HELOC (home equity line of credit) or cash-out refinance for a kitchen remodel, debt consolidation, etc.

The homeowner is essentially being gaslit into converting equity that already belongs to them into a new long-term loan that accrues interest all over again.

These ventures can make sense in rare, high-planned situations tied to high-returns but not in cases where the motive is discretionary. Saving for a large purchase takes longer than financing it yes, but it also provides security which a new, bigger loan just cannot.

No matter how fancy it looks. Debt servicers know how to market their products well. They disguise shackles as flexibility, but really they’re coming for the wealth you’ve already built while claiming to make more for you.

Your home equity is your net worth, not spendable cash. Unless “unlocking it” funds something that generates income or measurable value.

A fee-only advisor is your best friend when it comes to dealing with offers for HELOC or cash-out refinancing. Before you decide anything, compare the total interest cost to how much you could save in 12–24 months for the same purchase before signing anything. The number might surprise you.

Debt is not a moral failing. Nobody builds a career in medicine— or anything for that matter,  without borrowing something along the way. But building wealth that lasts (preferably for generations) requires you to differentiate between good and bad debt.

Student loans, a reasonable mortgage and car payments aside, if you find yourself dreading the monthly payments you know will eat chunks out of your salary, maybe a new plan is what you’re missing.

If any of this hits close to home, you don’t have to figure it out alone. The PoF community is here to help. Drop a comment or take a look at the resources on our site made specifically for this.

And if you’ve already beaten your debt, I want to hear from you. What actually worked? What almost derailed you? Share your story in the comments. Someone reading this today is looking for proof it’s possible— you’re it.

Yes. Almost nobody finishes medical school and residency debt free unless family money paid for it. The debt itself isn’t the red flag. What you do with your income once you start earning is.

The scariest thing on a physician’s desk this October is the fourth-quarter estimated tax worksheet, propped against a 403(b) statement that hasn’t moved since spring.

Most retirement articles are written for someone worried about running out of money. You should worry about that too. On top of it, you carry a problem the average saver never meets: a tax code that takes 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700, trims your itemized deductions once you get there, shrinks your SALT break somewhere past $505,000, and reaches two years backward to set your Medicare premiums.

Every mistake on this list costs a little more in that bracket.

This list is built for physicians with six figures before the comma, including those who collect some or all of it on a 1099.

Physicians are one of the few groups positioned to collect the maximum Social Security benefit, because most of you clear the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December. That makes claiming age a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month; the same worker gets $4,152 at full retirement age and roughly $5,181 by holding out until 70. Claiming early trims the benefit permanently (5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months, 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that), and every year you wait past full retirement age adds 8%.

Dr. Addams claimed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums shifts at $200 an hour. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480, so his own paycheck ate his benefit. (Social Security credits some of that back at full retirement age, but the cash-flow plan he built was toast.) Semi-retired physicians are exactly the people who keep earning after they file.

Two other quirks hit doctors harder. The formula averages your 35 highest-earning years, and residency plus a late start can leave early retirees with zeros in that average; the bend points in the formula soften the blow for high earners, but pull your record at ssa.gov before assuming anything.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a price no insurer will match.

A serious diagnosis or a family tree with short branches can justify claiming early. For a healthy 62-year-old internist with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

The textbook move as retirement approaches is to dial down risk. Physicians who take that advice too far end up with a portfolio that can’t outrun their withdrawals.

Run the timeline. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years or longer. A bond-heavy portfolio feels safe in year one and starts losing ground to inflation and withdrawals by year ten, which is why stocks still have to do some of the lifting deep into retirement.

High earners face a sneakier version of this mistake, and it lives in asset location. Taxable bond interest gets hit at ordinary rates. At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (which applies above $250,000 of modified AGI for married couples and has never been indexed for inflation), you hand close to 41 cents of every interest dollar to Washington before your state takes its cut.

Park bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b), hold broad stock index funds in taxable, and look at municipal bonds if you need fixed income outside retirement accounts.

How much stock is enough? That depends on your spending, your other income, and how well you sleep through a 25% drawdown. “As little as possible” is not an allocation.

Landmark Wealth Management puts the S&P 500’s annualized return from 1926 through 2024 at about 10.3%. It’s a lovely number, and nobody in history has received it in a straight line.

Sequence-of-returns risk turns a reasonable plan into a slasher film.

Two physicians retire with the same $4 million and the same 10-year average return. Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (who, it turns out, was not) retires into a bear market, sells shares near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back when prices recover. Same average, very different endings.

The 4% rule tries to account for that. William Bengen published it in 1994: withdraw 4% in year one, then adjust that dollar amount for inflation every year after. Bengen has since revised his own number upward to about 4.7%.

The real mistake is treating any single figure as permanent. Retirees who trim spending after bad years (guardrail strategies) or who keep two to three years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds (the bucket approach) give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Pick a method, stress-test it against a crash in year one, and expect to adjust it.

Read: Is the 4% Rule Too Frugal for Doctors?

Maxing your 401(k), 403(b), and 457(b) during peak earning years at 37% is a good move. The trouble starts when it’s the only move for 25 years.

Dr. Smart retires at 60 with $5 million, nearly all of it pre-tax. Required minimum distributions begin at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security, up to 85% of which is taxable.

Suddenly, a retired doctor is back in a high bracket, paying tax on money she deferred at a high bracket. Then Medicare notices.

Medicare’s IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at a modified AGI of $218,000 for couples ($109,000 single).

At the top tier, Part B jumps from the standard $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, which adds up to roughly $6,900 a year per person in surcharges alone. Medicare also uses a two-year look-back, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

The fix lives in the gap years. Retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade where taxable income is the lowest it’s been since residency. Converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth in that window, filling the lower brackets on purpose, shrinks future RMDs before they become a problem.

During your working years, fund backdoor Roth IRAs ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan.

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already made that choice for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions have to go in as Roth.

Rental income, a part-time medical director role, or expert witness work can also give you an income stream that doesn’t depend on draining one enormous tax-deferred account.

Physicians tend to underestimate retirement spending for a simple reason: they’ve never tracked it. The paycheck covered everything, so nobody looked.

Pull 12 months of actual spending from your cards and accounts, then adjust for what changes after medicine. Disability insurance, licensing fees, CME, and the commute fall away. Travel tends to swell and front-load into the first decade.

Healthcare before Medicare can run five figures a year for a couple buying their own coverage. Long-term care waits at the back of the line: Genworth figures cited in Fisher Investments’ healthcare guide put a semi-private nursing home room at roughly $111,000 a year in 2024, and federal estimates say almost 70% of people will need some form of long-term care, for about three years on average.

Errors cut in two directions. Underestimate spending, and you drain the portfolio early. Overestimate it, and you work three extra years you didn’t need, a loss that never shows up on any statement.

Anyone who practiced through 2022 watched CPI peak at 9.1% that June. Inflation cooled afterward, but prices never went back down.

The damage compounds quietly. A $200,000 annual retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation. Any income stream that doesn’t adjust (a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, a practice buyout paid in level installments) loses purchasing power every year you hold it.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician payment has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 once you adjust for inflation in practice costs. Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched happen to your fee schedule, and build in an inflation assumption a bit above whatever the current forecast says.

The urge to leave is real, and it’s showing up earlier. In Doximity’s physician polling, the share of doctors aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement rose between 2023 and 2026, from 30% to 46%. Among emergency physicians, the figure climbed from 30% to 52%.

Burnout is a legitimate reason to change your life and a poor reason to skip the math. Retiring at 52 instead of 60 means eight fewer years of contributions, eight extra years of withdrawals, and a longer stretch buying your own health insurance before Medicare.

Several costs belong to medicine alone. If your malpractice policy is claims-made, leaving can trigger a tail coverage bill, often priced at a multiple of your annual premium, unless your employer covers it or your carrier offers a free tail at retirement age.

A few years away can complicate credentialing if you want back in, and some boards will ask for a formal re-entry program.

On the brighter side, physicians have unusual access to early withdrawals: governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age, and the rule of 55 lets you tap the 401(k) or 403(b) of the employer you leave in or after the year you turn 55.

A middle path often beats a hard stop. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or moving into a nonclinical role keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow a few more years untouched.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger number, and a market dip convinces you to stay another year, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve thought about slowing down.

Dr. Addams (yes, him again) planned to retire at 62, then 64, then “once the kids finish school.” His youngest graduated in 2019. Money saved after you’ve crossed the finish line buys very little extra safety, and the years spent earning it come out of your healthiest stretch of life.

Hospitals are changing the math as well. Some now require cognitive and physical screening for late-career physicians past a set age, so the decision to keep practicing may not stay entirely yours.

Pick a number and a date, and write down what you’ll do the Monday after. In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those who are simply running from the pager.

This is the first of three entries that replace the generic advice, and it’s the one high earners ask me about most.

Long-term rentals generate depreciation, but for a full-time physician those losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income.

Short-term rentals play by different rules. If the average guest stay is seven days or less, the property isn’t treated as a rental activity under the regulations. Materially participate (most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more hours than any other individual) and the losses become non-passive, free to offset your W-2 or 1099 income.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, permanently restored by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act for property acquired after January 19, 2025, and the first-year numbers get large.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, depending on the property and the study. In the 37% bracket, that’s roughly $55,000 to $74,000 of federal tax that stays in your pocket.

The fine print, which the Instagram gurus skip, matters as much as the pitch:

If any of your income arrives on a 1099 (locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work, consulting), you have access to retirement accounts your W-2 colleagues can only envy.

Plenty of contractors open a SEP-IRA and stop there, which is an expensive default.

A Solo 401(k) usually beats it. For 2026, you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (a limit shared with any W-2 401(k) or 403(b) you also contribute to), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings as a sole proprietor, or 25% of W-2 salary through an S corporation, up to a combined $72,000.

Add $8,000 in catch-up contributions at 50, or $11,250 between ages 60 and 63. The employer side stands apart from your hospital plan, so an employed doc with meaningful side income can layer it on top of what they already contribute at work. The SEP has one more flaw for high earners: its balance counts under the pro-rata rule and sabotages the backdoor Roth.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan. It’s a defined benefit plan layered on top of the Solo 401(k), and allowable contributions rise with age, often into six figures a year for physicians in their 50s.

You’ll need an actuary and a funding commitment you can’t skip in a lean year, so it suits consistent earners.

Those deductions do double duty because of the QBI cliff. Physicians run a “specified service trade or business,” so the 20% qualified business income deduction phases out as taxable income rises.

For 2026, married couples get the full deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it vanishes entirely at $553,500 (the single thresholds are $201,750 and $276,750).

Dr. Lucky, married with roughly $500,000 of taxable 1099 income, sits deep in the phase-out. Fund the Solo 401(k) and a cash balance plan, drop taxable income below $403,500, and the QBI deduction rises from the dead on top of the retirement deduction itself.

Self-employment tax deserves a sentence of its own. Contractors pay the employee and employer shares of Social Security (12.4% combined) up to the $184,500 wage base and 2.9% Medicare on everything, plus another 0.9% above $250,000 for married couples.

An S corporation paying you a reasonable salary can trim part of that, though it adds payroll, a separate return, and a salary figure the IRS will scrutinize.

Physicians start saving late. Residency ends somewhere around 30 or 32, often with six-figure student debt, so the compounding years most savers get in their 20s went to call rooms and loan servicers. A year-end cram session can’t make that up.

The calendar matters more than usual this fall. These items won’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

Pick one item from this list before you hand out the first fun-size Snickers, and make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

The practical takeaway for me is to use the gap years for partial Roth conversions instead of leaving the whole tax problem for later.

#8680. JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy® (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

Not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

#8678. Tuition-Free College Classes for Seniors – The Catch Is Getting a Seat

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

In many states, public colleges waive tuition for residents once they reach 60, 62, or 65, so you can take regular college classes for little more than books and fees. Ask a nearby public college’s registrar for its tuition waiver for older students, and find out when waiver students may register.

That date decides what you can take, because waiver students usually get only the seats left after paying students sign up.

The other rules vary by state. Florida law lets the state’s public universities and colleges waive tuition and fees for residents 60 and older who audit classes, meaning they sit in without earning credit. At the University of North Georgia, Georgia residents 62 and older can take classes for credit or audit them, but they can’t register for fall or spring terms until the first day of classes. Kentucky law requires the state’s public colleges to waive all tuition and fees for residents 65 and older unless classes are full.

Under North Georgia’s waiver, a 66-year-old Georgia resident taking two history classes a semester pays for her books, supplies, and any lab fees, but no tuition.

To find your state’s version, call the registrar or continuing education office at a nearby public college and ask for its tuition waiver for older students. Bring proof of age and residency, such as a driver’s license, and ask whether you can earn credit and which fees you still owe. Where no nearby school offers one, ask your state’s higher education agency which campuses do.

If no seat opens, look up the nearest Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. The institutes, at colleges in all 50 states, run noncredit classes for people 50 and older, with no tests or grades, for fees that vary by institute. A community college’s continuing education classes and universities’ free online courses are other options.

For a waiver seat, call the registrar a semester ahead, since you may need to apply for admission by the college’s usual deadline before the waiver covers a class.
