“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. We have written an article on retirement that might compliment the informative blog here. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

They left out the annuity with a 5% rate guaranteed growth with step ups if the market does better than 5% minus fees. You can attach an ins package for your spouse. take a 4% W/D on your money. dont increase your standard of living to just be like everyone else. avoid the race to nowhere and stay away from out of state tuition. your kids will do well anywhere they go if they apply themselves: they got the intellect and drive from their parents not private school or private universities. Cars get you to and from work – where is the luxury? in the car dealerships pocket. Bigger houses dont mean happy homes and what do you do with the extra bedrooms when the adults start their own lives? Money left over after you max a 401k with a profit sharing plan (employ your spouse after the kids are gone), time to put extra into index funds with a downside sharing of risk. might not make the 14-19% that other are making but none of the panic when covid 2.0 comes to the shore. I went through 3 financial planners (all with vacation homes on my money) before I found Andrew. I was sold when he asked me a simple question. How much do you spend per month? Let’s see how much you have to have saved to make that per year with inflation. Its amazing how much you can love medicine when you can retire whenever the fancy hits you once you have attained the above goal!

They assume their income means they’re wealthy, then discover their spending ate everything.

The freedom you describe—loving medicine because you can retire whenever you want—that’s what happens when you get the math right early. You avoided the nightmare by doing exactly what Dr. Addams eventually learned: live below your means, ignore the Joneses, and make the boring financial moves that actually work.

#8656. Use Tax Software for Simple Returns – Pay a Pro for Rentals & Inheritances

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

File your own return with tax software when it holds W-2 pay, the standard deduction, common credits, or a simple side business. Pay a tax pro for a rental, an inheritance, a business sale, a home sale with a big profit, income from several states, stock pay, or an IRS letter you don’t understand.

Tax software asks you questions and does the math, and on a simple return you can answer them from your W-2, 1099s, and last year’s return.

H&R Block files a simple return free online, state included. A federal return that itemizes deductions, such as mortgage interest, costs $65 there, against $300 to $600 on average at accounting firms in a 2024 National Society of Accountants survey. Filers under an income limit can file a federal return free through IRS Free File.

A pro is worth paying where the right answer takes judgment, such as how much of a rental’s price was land or what an inherited house was worth when its owner died. Software accepts whatever you type.

A rental shows why a pro can be worth the fee. Say you’re in the 22% tax bracket, you start renting out a house in January, the building alone cost $220,000, and the rent nets $10,000 after other costs. Depreciation, the yearly deduction for a building’s wear, comes to about $7,700 that first year, which cuts your tax by about $1,700. Skip it, and you lose that $1,700 unless you fix it later, yet the IRS still adds the skipped depreciation to your taxable gain when you sell.

For a middle path, H&R Block’s paid tiers, from $65 plus $49 a state, include a tax pro on call, and TurboTax charges $59 to $209 plus state for its version. Or pay an online tax preparation service to do the whole return.

Start your return in tax software, and book a pro the moment it asks a question you’d have to guess at.

Compare the best free tax software to find a free tier that covers every form your return needs.

A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing

Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you plan a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on or around the 1st of each month. Set a calendar reminder. Follow Flying Blue on social media and sign up for their email newsletter — they announce the month's featured routes there. The ChooseFI community forums and travel rewards deal-tracking sites will also surface these announcements within minutes of release.

When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Note: Flying Blue's search only shows Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

Do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move quickly through the next steps.

From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

With miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Let's walk through a redemption that the ChooseFI community has actually executed.

The Route: New York (JFK) → Paris (CDG) in Business class on Air France

The Cash Price: A direct Air France Business class ticket on this route typically retails between $3,000 and $5,500 depending on the season. For this example, let's use a realistic mid-range price of $3,800.

The Promo Reward Price: 40,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, plus approximately $60–$80 in taxes and fees. No fuel surcharges — because it's a Promo award.

The CPP Calculation: $3,800 ÷ 40,000 miles = 9.5 cents per point. That's nearly 10x what you'd get using those same Chase points for cash back at 1 cent each.

You board at JFK and step into Air France's Business class cabin — the same product that Business travelers are paying $3,800+ to access. You have a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, a curated French menu with Champagne service before takeoff, noise-canceling headphones, an amenity kit, and pajamas on longer segments. The CDG lounge is yours before departure — the Air France lounge in Terminal 2E is a genuine culinary experience, not an airport afterthought. You land in Paris rested, not wrecked.

For a couple, you'd need 80,000 miles total — both ways would be 160,000 miles. A pair of Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve cardholders who signed up in the same year could realistically have this banked between welcome bonuses and everyday spend. Transfer from Chase to Flying Blue: instant. Time from decision to booking: under 15 minutes.

You did not pay $7,600 for two Business class tickets across the Atlantic. You paid 80,000 points and roughly $160 in fees. Those points cost you, at most, $800 in credit card spend if you valued them at 1 cent each — meaning you captured $7,440 in travel value from an $800 equivalent investment in points. That's the FI multiplier that makes this program worth mastering.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st

Flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns

Promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can plan your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

The ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

Couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

Minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

**Difficulty Rating: Hard — But for Specific, Solvable Reasons** This isn't hard because the booking process itself is complicated. Flyingblue.com is a functional, English-language booking tool that anyone can navigate. It's hard because of **timing and availability** — two factors that reward the prepared and punish the passive. **What Specifically Makes This Hard:** 1. **Monthly availability windows are brief.** You have 24–48 hours from the Promo announcement to act before the best dates disappear. If you're not watching, you miss the cycle entirely and wait another month. 2. **Dynamic pricing outside of Promo is punishing.** If you miss the Promo window and try to book a standard award on the same route, you could pay 2–3x more miles. The program's value is almost entirely concentrated in the monthly Promo structure. 3. **Coordination across accounts takes discipline.** Keeping 40,000–80,000 points liquid in a transferable account, not spending them on something else, and being ready to move instantly requires real points discipline. **Three Tips to Overcome the Challenge:** - **Automate your awareness.** Sign up for Flying Blue emails and follow deal-tracking communities so the announcement comes to you. - **Keep your points liquid in Chase or Amex.** The instant transfer speeds are your competitive advantage over slower-moving transfer paths. - **Be route-flexible, not date-flexible.** You may not get Paris in July, but you might get Amsterdam in September — and that's still an extraordinary redemption. If you're willing to build the habit of checking on the 1st of each month and keeping a points buffer ready, the hard part becomes routine. The ChooseFI community has proven this works — repeatedly.

Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com and enable email notifications. Keep at least 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in your Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt account. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.

Visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

Use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates quickly.

Transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

Promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. A business class transatlantic award that normally costs 80,000 to 100,000 miles one-way can drop to 40,000 to 50,000 miles on a Promo Reward. Additionally, fuel surcharges are eliminated on promo awards, saving another $100 to $300 per ticket that would otherwise be charged on standard awards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards and Citi ThankYou are the best because they transfer instantly to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

Yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

The best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Keep 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in reserve, check on the 1st of every month, and book the moment you find a route that matches your travel list. Over time, this single strategy can deliver thousands of dollars in business class experiences at economy-level points costs.

#8654. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment)

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more quickly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45)

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the big tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:

Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

Great question! The fundamental idea of index funding is “Absolutely Not!” – for at least three reasons:

1) Because that shift of money into the big 7 tech companies has already happened. They’re valued at EIGHTEEN TRILLION DOLLARS!! 2) By continuing to own just the index, you will continue to participate in any growth of these companies, as well as all the unexpected rising stars yet to come. 3) Because actively jumping out of the index into individual stocks in an attempt to outperform the market is a proven losing strategy. Everybody thinks they know better, they don’t, collectively they fall into a random distribution and their overall performance defines “the market”.

Not an expert so I may be wrong about this, but I think this is how it would work: Suppose Tesla swallows Uber. If you own an index fund linked to S&P 500, you own both, through that index fund, and your indirectly-held Uber shares get converted to indirectly-held Tesla shares – and typically when a company buys another company, it does it at a price above the market rate, so the number of Tesla shares you’d get is going to be better than if you sold Uber and bought Tesla before the deal.

If you’ve got a broad-based market index and one company eats most of the world economy, as long as you’ve got shares in that company and shares in most of the companies it buys and incorporates into itself, which you would have through a broad-based market index, you should be fine.

I have other worries regarding the future where there are a bunch of smarter-than-the-average-human machines around, because I figure that leads to bigger changes than “maybe the stock market does something weird”, but that’s a comment for a different blog.

Is Buy and Hold Always the Best Strategy? History Says… Not Always. Yes, over the last few decades, the buy-and-hold strategy has worked incredibly well, with U.S. stock markets delivering strong returns. But that hasn’t always been the case. There have been entire decades where buy and hold yielded little to no real returns—or worse.

The 1930s: The Great Depression saw the Dow Jones lose nearly 90% of its value from 1929 to 1932. Even though the market eventually recovered, it took 25 years (until 1954) for stocks to fully regain their pre-crash levels.

The 1970s: Stagflation (high inflation + stagnant growth) crushed stock returns. The S&P 500 gained only 5% total from 1969 to 1979, which was a negative real return after inflation.

The 2000s: After the Dot-Com bubble burst in 2000 and the Financial Crisis of 2008, the S&P 500 produced negative total returns from 2000 to 2009—dubbed the “Lost Decade” for stocks.

While stocks historically tend to rise over long periods, these examples show that timing, valuation, and diversification matter. Simply buying and holding without considering macroeconomic conditions or valuations can lead to lost decades for investors

Mr. Money Mustache February 25, 2025, 10:34 am

Some of those stories about past periods of low stock returns are true, but I encourage readers to remember three more things:

1) They are usually cherry picked, for example starting from the exact peak of the 1929 bubble. In reality, investors at the time had probably accumulated most of their investments at lower prices, so they were net-positive far sooner than 1954

2) Many of the analyses you see online happen to leave out the most important reason we own stocks in the long run: DIVIDENDS – so ensure that any past simulations you run are using a data set that includes dividends (Nick Maggiulli from Of Dollars and Data is a great author who understands this: https://ofdollarsanddata.com/sp500-calculator/)

3) It’s easy to tell stories about the past and imagine that we all have a crystal ball. But remember that people back then had NO IDEA when the crash would come. In fact, I have been receiving emails non-stop since I 2013, shortly after I started writing this blog stating that it’s “time to go to cash because the market is overvalued”. In retrospect, not only our share prices but our economic growth and company earnings have been spectacular since then.

And perhaps most importantly 4) Ten years is a TINY time horizon to be thinking about investment performance for FIRE people. I’m personally less than a third of the way through my seventy year retirement, so I think in much longer time periods. A 10-15 year stretch of minimal stock growth is all built into the safety margin.

There is definitely a limit to how much a nation can safely borrow as a percentage of GDP. But this is very different from the crap the politicians sling around to rile up their base and justify cutting the programs they just happen to dislike for ideological reasons.

In a worldwide currency and debt market like we have, if you borrow too much the market sends you a signal in the form of lower demand for your dollars which leads to a decline in your currency’s value. Then you need to offer higher interest rates in order to keep borrowing money.

In recent decades the US has had the opposite “problem” – we issue higher and higher amounts of debt for sale, and buyers keep vacuuming it up which keeps our dollar strong. So like a drunk teen at the liquor store with his Mom’s credit card, we keep taking advantage of the free sauce.

To the extent that our government uses this borrowed money to build infrastructure that actually helps our country: transportation networks, ports, power production, educating our populace, even incentivizing things like Arizona semiconductor fabs, we are actually getting ahead because we are using other people’s money to build our own wealth.

It can also help to use this implicit subsidy to just lower taxes on businesses and average workers, because this will trigger more company formation and wealth and employment.

But if we go too far and see our dollar drop more than we want *or* lose our status as the world’s reserve currency, we will have to go on a serious spending diet.

But the issue is best discussed by a group of well trained economists and business leaders with a set of spreadsheets rather than a shouting political candidate at a rally.

The best approach is somewhere in between: run a sensible budget, but also bend the rules a bit and borrow a safe amount for the long run to continue juicing our own economy.

Brian Slattery February 25, 2025, 11:27 am

The results were cherry picked except for the people that retired at the start of those periods. For them it was real!

For the early ’70s retiree, the 4% rule just about held up, but with little margin for error. Wade Pfau’s international study found that for a 50/50 portfolio in U.S. history, 4% was roughly the “Safemax” (worst-case sustainable rate) – it survived about 30 years by the skin of its teeth, supporting only ~29 years of inflation-adjusted withdrawals in the most challenging stretch​ RETIREMENTRESEARCHER.COM . In practical terms, this means a 4% initial withdrawal did eventually work out for a 1970s retiree but only because subsequent decades (the 1980s and 1990s) were very strong. The retiree would have seen their nest egg shrink alarmingly in the first 5–10 years, likely coming close to depletion by the early 1980s, before the tide turned. T. Rowe Price analysts, for instance, note that a 1973 retiree’s portfolio (with a roughly 4% starting withdrawal) began at $500k, sank to ~$328k by 1974, but then recovered to over $500k by 1982 and ultimately grew to over $1 million by the end of 30 years​ TROWEPRICE.COM ​ TROWEPRICE.COM . In hindsight the 4% rule “worked” for that retiree – but if inflation had stayed high longer or if the 1980s boom had been weaker, the outcome could have been a failure.

It’s not a coincidence that the 4% rule just barely worked for 1970s retirees. That was the worst time period for investors in the 20th century, and 4% was chosen because it’s the maximum withdrawal rate that survived even that period.

The thing that I find interesting is all the doomsayers (i.e., those prognosticating some sort of nigh-apocalyptic destruction of the stock market) seem to operate under this bizarre assumption that the behemoths (i.e., the Magnificent 7 and others near the top of the pile) are just going to sit there and allow themselves to get trampled by some upstart. Or that they will just shrug their shoulders, say something like “well, I guess it was fun while it lasted, time to pack up the toys and go home” and then it will all be over.

Will there be disruption? Absolutely! Will it somehow upend the US stock market? I highly doubt that. The companies in the S&P 500 are economic engines, and their fuel is not just natural resources from Canada, Brazil, and Russia, but also other smaller companies. As soon as some small company comes along with a potentially disruptive change, you will absolutely see the big boys try to get in on the game (both by attempting to acquire the upstart, and also by starting or accelerating their own efforts in that space).

There is a good chance that some of the economic benefit will be “lost” (i.e., those who get in early will reap an outsized gain, while those of us index-only investors will have to wait for that disruptive technology to go mainstream), but in the end that disruptive technology will become *part* of the engine of our economy, rather than wrecking it.

My question is what happens in countries where monopolies control those things and stomp out competition due to undue bought influence from the government? In that case, the naturally self-correcting mechanisms don’t work, and political capital controls the top companies, rather than true innovation driving the market.

I suppose those companies would still be making record profits, though, so it may be a moot point.

Y axis is S&P500. On x-axis, Year 0 means “right now”. The x-axis means “future”. The red line starts below yellow and blue because stocks are overvalued, i.e. have a higher P/E. The red shows what S&P SHOULD BE if P/E was typical, not very high as it is now. Basically, if the market crashed right now and reversed to a normal P/E. The blue line shows what S&P would be in the future if the current trends continue (unlikely). As mentioned above, the red line shows what S&P future will be if stocks would suddenly revert to a typical P&E now. The yellow line is similar to the red line, but shows a more gradual reversal to typical P/Es, over time. M&Ms point is that even the worse case scenario – red line – is still pretty good.

I’ve started investing about 8 years ago. I’ve decided, and stuck with, a two prong approach. Half in well known index etf’s, half in about 20 handpicked stocks that I liked. If i screw up myself, I would still have the etf’s. For my own hand picked stocks, I choose to stick to about 20 stocks. Research has shown multiple times that 20 stocks will yield the same results as an index consisting of hundreds or even thousands of stocks. You don’t need an index, you just need 20 random stocks and they’ll perform the same.

My 20 stocks I keep as a hobby and to learn about new companies, how companies are run, new insights etc. It keeps me interested in the stockmarket. The stocks that I pick are companies I’m familiar with, or believe will do well. I avoid hype like the plague. I avoid high PE’s. I try to follow Buffets advice as best I can. Don’t loose money. Buy low, sell never or at least very high.

I’ve sold Tesla at a loss in 2019, never owned it again. I’ve never owned Meta, Amazon, Apple, Nvidia. Or AMD, or any other recent 10bagger. I have stuck with boring, mostly relatively unknown stocks. Or where I saw a real opportunity.

The real kicker? About 70% of the stocks are European. I barely own any US stocks.

The results: My own hand picked 20 stocks have done better than the S&P500.

I’m not a great stock picker. I didn’t invest in NVidia, Google, AMD. I sold Tesla at a loss before it went time 20. I still hold a 50% on a significant Intel stake. I stuck to Europe while the US outperformed. And yet, my returns have beaten the S&P500.

There are some great stocks in Europe. There is also a lot of not so great stocks. Picking the great ones isn’t hard. Most can see the bad ones from far away and avoid them like the plague.

The real problem for Europe, is the lack of representative indexes. The European indexes just simply suck. Not enough stocks in them. Every country has their own indexes of just a few stocks. And maybe an even bigger underappreciated problem comparing the US to the EU: dividends. The US companies barely pay dividends, while EU companies still pay a good deal. The difference adds up over the years, but most indexes don’t compare the total return.

As for these high markets: please keep in mind: we’ve had some serious inflation. Inflation adjusted returns over the last years aren’t out of the ordinary. Especially comparing inflation adjusted returns to something like a zero risk tips ladder.

Your S&P500 without the magnificent seven looks less impressive. But instead of taking out the best performers, maybe do the same but also take out the absolute worst performers. And then do both. You might be surprised to learn the whole market is actually doing really pretty well.

Conclusion: I’m really not worried. Taking a broader look and accounting for inflation and zero risk treasuries, returns aren’t extraordinary. We live in a world where in one generation, huge countries go from poor to rich, and they all want stable investments for their retirements. We live in an age where a growing number of retires will keep demand high because they don’t have to fear for their incomes. House payments look high, but the total mortgage debt in many western countries is actually quite low.

If there ever was a golden age, it’s now. We’re deadsmack in the middle of the best economic boom in history, and it doesn’t seem to be ending anytime soon (if you take a worldwide broad look). Don’t focus too much on the numbers. Look around the world, see how much things are improving in just one generation world wide. You can only conclude demand for stocks will keep increasing, and companies will keep improving profits as demand keeps increasing. Will there be shock and crashes? Sure, but nothing to worry about for a early retiree.

I also like to think of the property pay down as an after tax return, since you need to earn the money first , then pay taxes to pay the mortgage.

#8653. Trick or Treatment: The Spookiest Things Physicians Learn About Being Human

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.
